title: "3.11 Testing code that touches a database"
description: "Test database code against a real Postgres, give every test a clean slate with transaction rollback, build test data with small factory functions, and run it all in CI."

::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 3 · Lesson 11 · About 60 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: a rehearsal stage that resets itself"}
Actors rehearse on a stage set that looks exactly like the real one, because a cardboard prop behaves differently from the real thing. After each scene a crew puts every object back in place, so the next scene starts identically. Database tests need the same two things: the **real** database (not a stand-in that behaves differently), and an automatic **reset** after every test.
:::

## Why a real Postgres

In lesson 2.6 you faked GitHub with `httpx.MockTransport`. Why not fake the database too? Because Atlas's database code *is* its behaviour: the `tsvector` column, `websearch_to_tsquery`, unique constraints and cascading deletes all happen inside Postgres. A fake would test your fake, not Atlas. And SQLite (lesson 3.9's stretch) lacks the features Atlas uses.

The rule this course follows: **fake what you don't own and can't control (GitHub, AI models), use the real thing for what you do own (your database)**.

## A separate test database

Tests must never touch your development data. Create a database just for them:

```text
$ docker compose exec db psql -U atlas -d atlas -c "create database atlas_test;"
CREATE DATABASE
```

and tell the tests where it is through an environment variable:

```bash
export TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://atlas:atlas-dev-password@localhost:5432/atlas_test
```

## The fixtures

Two fixtures in `tests/conftest.py` do all the work:

```python
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def engine() -> Iterator[Engine]:
    """One engine for the whole test run, on a database used only by tests."""
    url = os.environ.get("TEST_DATABASE_URL")
    if url is None:
        pytest.skip("set TEST_DATABASE_URL to run database tests (see lesson 3.11)")

    engine = create_engine(url)
    # Start from empty tables every run, whatever a previous run left behind.
    Base.metadata.drop_all(engine)
    Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
    yield engine
    engine.dispose()


@pytest.fixture
def session(engine: Engine) -> Iterator[Session]:
    """A session whose changes are rolled back after each test.

    The test's own commits become savepoints inside one outer transaction,
    so every test starts from the same empty tables and tests never interfere.
    """
    with engine.connect() as connection:
        transaction = connection.begin()
        session = Session(bind=connection, join_transaction_mode="create_savepoint")
        try:
            yield session
        finally:
            session.close()
            transaction.rollback()
```

- `scope="session"` makes the `engine` fixture run **once per test run**, not once per test: creating the tables once is much faster. (Here "session" is pytest's word for the whole test run, unrelated to a SQLAlchemy session.)
- A fixture that `yield`s runs the code after `yield` when the test finishes, like a `finally` (lesson 1.11 used `tmp_path`, which works the same way internally).
- `pytest.skip(...)` turns a missing database into skipped tests with a clear reason, instead of a crash. The other tests still run.

### The rollback trick

Each test gets a session bound to a connection whose **outer transaction is never committed**. When the test ends, `transaction.rollback()` undoes everything the test did.

But the code under test may itself commit (or call `session.begin()`). `join_transaction_mode="create_savepoint"` handles that: inside the test, a commit only releases a **savepoint** (a bookmark inside the outer transaction) instead of really committing.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  participant F as session fixture
  participant DB as Postgres (atlas_test)
  participant T as test
  F->>DB: BEGIN (outer transaction)
  F->>T: session
  T->>DB: INSERT documents, chunks ... (inside a savepoint)
  T->>DB: SELECT ... (sees its own rows)
  T-->>F: test finished (pass or fail)
  F->>DB: ROLLBACK (everything the test did disappears)
```

After the whole suite, the test database is empty again:

```text
 repos | documents | issues
-------+-----------+--------
     0 |         0 |      0
```

Rolling back is far faster than deleting rows or recreating tables for each test, and it means test order never matters.

## Small factory functions

Tests need realistic objects with sensible defaults. A tiny **factory function** keeps each test focused on what matters to *it*:

```python
def make_issue(number: int, labels: tuple[str, ...], days_old: int = 1) -> github.Issue:
    return github.Issue(
        number=number,
        title=f"Issue {number}",
        url=f"https://github.com/pytorch/ignite/issues/{number}",
        author="contributor",
        labels=labels,
        comments=0,
        created_at=datetime(2026, 11, 17, tzinfo=UTC) - timedelta(days=days_old),
    )
```

A test then reads like the behaviour it checks:

```python
def test_save_issues_inserts_updates_and_removes_closed(session: Session) -> None:
    storage.save_issues(session, "pytorch/ignite", [make_issue(1, ("bug",)), make_issue(2, ())])

    storage.save_issues(session, "pytorch/ignite", [make_issue(2, ("docs",))])

    stored = session.scalars(select(Issue)).all()
    assert [issue.number for issue in stored] == [2]
    assert [label.name for label in stored[0].labels] == ["docs"]
```

The dates are fixed (17 November 2026), not `datetime.now()`, so the test gives the same result on any day (lesson 1.11: no dependence on the outside world).

## What the storage tests cover

The `sample_repo` fixture from lesson 1.11 (a tiny fake codebase in `tmp_path`) feeds the indexing tests, so they don't depend on your Ignite clone:

```text
tests/test_storage.py::test_split_into_chunks_covers_every_line_once PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_index_stores_documents_and_chunks PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_reindexing_replaces_instead_of_duplicating PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_documents_are_classified_as_code_or_doc PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_find_ranks_matching_chunks_with_line_ranges PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_find_uses_word_stems PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_find_only_searches_the_named_repo PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_chunk_text_is_searchable_through_generated_column PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_save_issues_inserts_updates_and_removes_closed PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_labels_are_shared_not_duplicated PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_label_counts_most_common_first PASSED
tests/test_storage.py::test_age_buckets_include_empty_buckets PASSED
============================== 12 passed in 0.38s ==============================
```

Twelve database tests in under half a second. Two of these tests failed when first written, and both failures taught something:

- **Ordering.** A test expected paths in Python's order (`README.md` first), but this Postgres sorts text ignoring case (`ignite/...` first). The test now compares sets, because the order of those rows wasn't the behaviour under test.
- **Code search.** "fire event" found nothing, which led to the punctuation fix in lesson 3.6. A test found a real product bug before any user did.

Without `TEST_DATABASE_URL`, the database tests are skipped with their reason, and everything else still runs:

```text
SKIPPED [1] tests/test_storage.py:103: set TEST_DATABASE_URL to run database tests (see lesson 3.11)
36 passed, 11 skipped in 0.27s
```

## Running it in CI

A skipped test protects nothing. In CI the database tests must always run, so `.github/workflows/ci.yml` starts a Postgres **service container** next to the test job:

```yaml
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: atlas
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: atlas-test-password
          POSTGRES_DB: atlas_test
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U atlas -d atlas_test"
          --health-interval 2s
          --health-retries 15
    env:
      TEST_DATABASE_URL: postgresql+psycopg://atlas:atlas-test-password@localhost:5432/atlas_test
```

It's the same idea as `compose.yml` (lesson 3.1), in GitHub Actions' format: start Postgres 17, wait until it's healthy, then run the job with `TEST_DATABASE_URL` set. CI is covered properly in lesson 7.2.

## Common mistakes

- **Tests sharing a database with development**: one `drop_all` and your data is gone.
- **Tests that pass alone but fail together**, because one test's rows leak into another. Rollback per test prevents it.
- **Tests asserting on row order without `ORDER BY`**, or on an order the database's text sorting decides.
- **`datetime.now()` in test data**, making results depend on the day.
- **Silently skipping in CI.** Make CI provide the database so the skip never happens there.

## Check yourself

**1.** Why doesn't Atlas fake the database in tests the way it fakes GitHub?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Much of Atlas's behaviour (full-text search, constraints, cascades) happens inside Postgres, so a fake would only test the fake. GitHub is external, rate-limited and changes; Atlas's own database is fully under its control and fast to run locally.
:::

**2.** What does `join_transaction_mode="create_savepoint"` solve?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Code under test may commit. With this mode, those commits only release savepoints inside the fixture's outer transaction, so the final rollback still undoes everything the test did.
:::

**3.** A test uses `datetime.now()` to create an issue "3 days old" and checks it's in the "under 30 days" bucket. What could go wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Probably nothing on most days, but the test now depends on the clock: if the code and the test compute "now" slightly differently, or the boundaries change, it can fail unpredictably. Fixed dates, with "now" passed in as a parameter (as `age_buckets` does), make it deterministic.
:::

## Exercise

Write a test proving that deleting a repo deletes its documents **and their chunks** (the `ON DELETE CASCADE` chain from lesson 3.4). Index `sample_repo`, delete the `Repo` row, flush, and count chunks.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from sqlalchemy import delete


def test_deleting_a_repo_cascades_to_documents_and_chunks(
    session: Session, sample_repo: Path
) -> None:
    storage.index_folder(session, "pytorch/ignite", sample_repo)

    session.execute(delete(Repo).where(Repo.full_name == "pytorch/ignite"))
    session.flush()

    assert session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Document)) == 0
    assert session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(Chunk)) == 0
```

A bulk `delete()` statement goes straight to the database, so it's Postgres's foreign-key cascade that removes the children: exactly what the test is meant to prove.
:::

## Stretch

Add a test that the database **rejects** a chunk whose `start_line` is after its `end_line`. Use `pytest.raises(IntegrityError)` (from `sqlalchemy.exc`) around a `session.flush()`. Why must the test flush?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError


def test_chunk_line_range_is_enforced(session: Session, sample_repo: Path) -> None:
    storage.index_folder(session, "pytorch/ignite", sample_repo)
    document = session.scalars(select(Document)).first()
    assert document is not None

    session.add(Chunk(document_id=document.id, start_line=10, end_line=5, text="x"))
    with pytest.raises(IntegrityError):
        session.flush()
```

`session.add` alone sends nothing to the database; the `CHECK` constraint only fires when the `INSERT` runs, which is at flush (or commit). After a database error, the session must be rolled back before it's usable again; the fixture's final rollback takes care of that.
:::

## What changed in the project

`my-atlas` has database fixtures in `conftest.py`, a `test_storage.py` suite, and a CI job that runs it against a real Postgres. Commit: `test: Covered storage against a real Postgres`.
